title: Refined Estimation of Effluent Intrusion Magnitude: Implications for China's Drinking Water Source Protection
content:
Abstract

The United Nations' 2030 Agenda prioritizes “Clean Water and Sanitation”, yet urbanization and expansion of centralized wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are increasingly discharging treated effluents into natural waters and drinking water sources (DWSs). This intrusion is driven by a combination of factors, including spatial distribution of WWTPs, effluent volumes, river network structure, and hydrological connectivity. China, home to the world's largest and most extensive WWTP networks, faces growing risks of such effluent impacts on rivers and the DWSs, particularly concerning emerging contaminants that persist post-treatment. In this study, we develop a high-resolution analytical framework integrating Python and ArcGIS to quantify effluent transport from 10,826 WWTPs across 578,506 river segments (2.46 × 106 km) to 894 DWSs. Our model calculates seasonal effluent contributions and quantifies transport distances and times from outfalls to DWSs. Results show that 9.91% of river lengths and 39.15% of DWSs are affected by effluent, with 21.48% of DWSs exceeding the 10% dry-season safety threshold. Hydrological regimes critically modulate risks: wet-season transport is faster (median: 1.76 hr) with lower median effluent contribution (2.44%), whereas dry-season transport is slower (median: 13.94 hr) but contributes more (median: 15.09%). Elevated wet-season risks arise from shortened travel times and reduced dilution capacity. Meeting China's 2040 water reuse target could reduce effluent impacts in DWSs by 36.08% (to median 11.26% in dry season). This study clarifies effluent impacts on China's DWSs and supports urban water security, highlighting implications for developing nations with regulatory gaps in managing such risks.
